strengths: Clear and compelling conceptual contribution: the paper redefines what 'true' novel view synthesis means via transferability, identifies that prior self-supervised NVS models (RayZer, RUST) act as frame interpolators rather than NVS models, and provides a clean formalization (Secs. 3.1–3.3) including the True Pose Similarity metric that the community can adopt.

The proposed method is well-motivated and simple: the stereo-monocular design eliminates the interpolation path, and the pose-preserving augmentation strategy (two inverse masks on the same sequence) elegantly converts the transferability criterion into a tractable self-supervised training objective for real-world video.

Large-scale, diverse evaluation across four real-world datasets (RE10K, DL3DV, MVImgNet, CO3Dv2) at both scene and object levels, with large quantitative margins over baselines (AUC@20° more than 5x RayZer/RUST) plus qualitative trajectory visualizations.

Thorough and informative ablations (Table 3) that isolate the contributions of the stereo-monocular design and the transferability objective, including the counter-intuitive and interesting finding that explicit SE(3) parameterization and Plücker embeddings degrade transferability relative to unconstrained latents.

Honest treatment of limitations (wide-baseline stereo constraint, deterministic rendering artifacts), transparent reporting of the autoencoding benchmark for completeness, and a useful probe analysis (Table 2) showing pose latents correlate with oracle SE(3) poses.
weaknesses: All baseline comparisons rely on the authors' re-implementations. While the RayZer implementation was confirmed faithful by its authors, the RUST implementation is explicitly modified (no set-latent scene representation), making the RUST comparison partially a comparison against a derived variant rather than the published method.

The transferability evaluation (TPS) depends on VGGT as the ORACLE. Any systematic biases or failures of VGGT propagate directly into the headline metric, and no analysis of the oracle's reliability or error bars/confidence intervals on the reported metrics is provided.

Rendering quality remains modest relative to pose-supervised methods (e.g., PSNR ~26 on RE10K at 256x256) with acknowledged blurring/warping artifacts, so the practical impact of 'true' NVS here is currently limited to controllability rather than photorealism.

Several design details are heuristic and under-analyzed: the mask construction from image quadrants, the small probability of skipping augmentation, the 'middlest' reference-frame selection, and dataset-specific baseline heuristics; sensitivity to these choices is not quantified.

The scalability path beyond two-view pose estimation is left open (multi-view POSEENC with self-supervision destroys transferability), which limits how far the approach currently extends; position relative to latent action models is discussed only briefly.
No code release is mentioned at submission time, which hampers reproducibility given the reliance on custom re-implementations of baselines and a bespoke evaluation protocol.

strengths: The paper introduces a clear and well-motivated conceptual reframing: 'transferability' as the defining property of true novel view synthesis, and formalizes it within a latent-variable decomposition of NVS systems (POSEENC / SCENEENC / RENDER). This framing is crisp and provides a useful lens for analyzing prior self-supervised methods.

The proposed True Pose Similarity (TPS) metric is a sensible, quantifiable operationalization of transferability, and the paper is admirably honest about its limitations (e.g., that it can be hacked and must be paired with perceptual checks).
The empirical diagnosis that RayZer and RUST learn interpolation latents rather than transferable poses is a valuable and non-obvious finding for the self-supervised NVS sub-area.

The counter-intuitive ablation result — that explicit SE(3) parameterization actually degrades transferability relative to unconstrained latents — is interesting and challenges a common design assumption.

Experiments span four large-scale real-world datasets at both scene and object level, and the ablation table is reasonably comprehensive, covering bottlenecking, SE(3) heads, and progressive re-introduction of multi-view context.
Training details (architecture, optimizer, compute, dataset baselines) are documented in the appendix, which supports partial reproducibility of the method itself.
weaknesses: All baseline comparisons rely on the authors' own reimplementations of RayZer and RUST, neither of which has released code. While the RayZer implementation was reportedly confirmed faithful by its authors, the RUST implementation deviates from the original design (no set-latent scene representation, modified POSEENC/RENDER split). The headline claim of 'dramatically outperforming' prior work therefore rests on comparisons the community cannot easily verify, and there is a risk the baselines were under-tuned relative to XFactor.

The central 'first fully self-supervised model to achieve true NVS' claim depends heavily on the authors' own definition of true NVS (transferability). The paper presents this definition as settled, but it is a reframing that deserves more careful justification and discussion of alternative formulations (e.g., controllability via canonical pose estimation, or latent action models which the paper itself acknowledges are related).

The proposed transferability objective relies on pose-preserving augmentations (complementary masks, color jitter, blur) applied to the same underlying frame pair. Because both augmented pairs derive from the identical source images, substantial pixel content remains shared across the pairs (e.g., a quadrant visible unmasked in augmentation A may appear in augmentation B's target), leaving a residual channel for content smuggling through the pose latent. The paper does not quantify how much content leakage remains, nor does it test alternative mask granularities or augmentation schemes.

Transferability results, while clearly better than baselines, are still modest in absolute terms: translation accuracy at 10° is only ~64-67% on three of four datasets, and CO3Dv2 AUC@10° is 14.0. The paper acknowledges blur/warping artifacts that worsen with baseline, stemming from the deterministic formulation — meaning the practical utility of the transferred trajectories in a real NVS pipeline is limited. The significance of the contribution partly hinges on whether the remaining gap is a matter of scale, which is not established.

The evaluation protocol for the transferability test is under-specified: how the 4000 pairs of sequences are drawn, how ORACLE (VGGT) errors on rendered (possibly blurry/warped) frames propagate into TPS, and how sensitive the ranking is to the choice of ORACLE are not analyzed. Since TPS is the paper's central metric, this is a meaningful soundness gap.

Key related directions are treated only briefly: pose-free methods with geometric priors (NoPoSplat-class, SelfSplat, FlowCam) are excluded by definition, which is defensible, but the paper would benefit from at least an oracle-supervised upper bound (e.g., LVSM-style model with VGGT poses) to contextualize how far self-supervised transferable NVS is from the supervised ceiling.
No code or project page content appears to be released ('Project Page:' is empty), which limits reproducibility of a paper whose contribution is partly a new metric and evaluation protocol.

Writing issues: several typos and informal phrasings ('less clear', 'act an interpolator', 'middlest', 'gives liase', 'pacification of the target image'), and the naming derivation 'Transferable[X] Latent Factorization[Factor]' is opaque. The mask augmentation description (quadrant partitioning) gives only four mask families, which seems too limited to fully minimize content overlap, yet this is not ablated.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated conceptual contribution: the paper identifies 'transferability' as the defining property of true NVS and formalizes it cleanly within a latent-variable framework, providing a principled reframing of self-supervised NVS as a pure machine learning problem.

The proposed XFactor method is well-designed: bootstrapping multi-view NVS from a stereo-monocular model to eliminate interpolative shortcuts, combined with a pose-preserving augmentation scheme (inverse masking) to realize the transferability objective on real-world video, is a clever and practical combination.

Extensive evaluation: results span four diverse real-world datasets (RE10K, DL3DV, MVImgNet, CO3Dv2), with a new quantitative metric (TPS), pose probing experiments against oracle SE(3) poses, and thorough ablations that isolate the contributions of the stereo-monocular design and the transferability objective.

The ablations are genuinely informative and support the paper's counterintuitive claims, e.g., that explicit SE(3) parameterization degrades transferability and that adding context views progressively destroys it.

The paper is honest about limitations (wide-baseline pose estimation, deterministic rendering artifacts) and includes autoencoding benchmarks for completeness, showing XFactor remains competitive on the standard RayZer benchmark.
Substantial training effort (large-scale data, multiple GPUs, fair compute-matched comparisons with standardized context view counts) suggests results are not artifacts of under-training baselines.
weaknesses: Both primary baselines (RayZer and RUST) are re-implementations rather than official code, and the RUST implementation intentionally deviates from the original; while the authors claim RayZer's authors confirmed faithfulness, this weakens the strength of the central 'prior methods fail transferability' claim.

The TPS metric is defined by the authors, and the proposed method is explicitly designed to optimize the very property this metric measures, creating a potential circularity concern; the probing experiments mitigate but do not fully remove this issue.

The pose-preserving augmentations (masking, color-jitter, blur) are synthetic perturbations of a single sequence, so the 'transferability objective' is trained on pairs that share identical content/pose by construction; how well this transfers to genuinely different real-world pairs with shared trajectories is not directly validated.

Absolute rendering quality remains moderate (e.g., translation accuracy at 10° is only ~35-67% on CO3Dv2, and the authors acknowledge blurring/warping artifacts for divergent target poses), so the method is far from replacing geometric approaches in practical use.

The 'first fully self-supervised model capable of true NVS' claim rests on the authors' own definition of true NVS, which some reviewers may view as a self-serving reframing of the task rather than a community-accepted criterion.
No code release is mentioned, limiting reproducibility given that no official baselines exist and the method involves several nontrivial design details.
The reference frame selection heuristic ('middlest') and other design choices appear heuristic without ablation support.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated conceptual contribution: identifying 'transferability' (the ability to reuse pose latents extracted from one sequence to re-render the same trajectory in a different scene) as the defining property of true NVS is a compelling reframing, and the latent-variable formulation in Sec. 3 makes the argument precise.

The proposed method is elegant and well-motivated: bootstrapping from a stereo-monocular model to prevent interpolation, combined with a pose-preserving augmentation scheme that enables a transferability objective on real-world video without any oracle supervision. The insight that forced SE(3) parameterization actually hurts transferability is a surprising and useful finding.

Introduction of the True Pose Similarity (TPS) metric fills a genuine gap — prior work evaluated self-supervised NVS only via autoencoding, which cannot distinguish true NVS from frame interpolation. The metric is standardized (RRA/RTA/AUC) and the authors thoughtfully probe oracle robustness (VGGT vs. COLMAP, Tables 7-9).

Comprehensive and convincing evaluation: large margins over RayZen and RUST across four real-world datasets (e.g., >5x AUC@20 in transferability), extensive ablations isolating each design decision (stereo-monocular vs. multi-view, bottleneck vs. unconstrained latents, SE(3) vs. unconstrained, transferability vs. SimCLR/VICReg objectives), and robustness analyses of the transferability objective under corruption.

Honest and detailed limitations section (wide-baseline restriction, blurring/warping artifacts, deterministic rendering), plus disclosure of baseline reimplementation details and confirmation of faithfulness with the RayZen authors.
Reproducibility: complete architecture details (Appendix A), training hyperparameters, dataset construction, and reasonable compute footprint (4-8 H200 GPUs).
weaknesses: The central claim of being the 'first true NVS' model relies on a criterion (transferability) that the authors themselves define, introducing some circularity risk. While the criterion is well-motivated, a skeptical reader could argue the paper defines the goalpost and then scores itself on it; stronger external validation (e.g., user studies on whether transferred trajectories look correct to humans) would help.

Evaluation depends heavily on the VGGT oracle, itself a large pre-trained structure-from-motion model. Although the method is trained without oracles, the measurement of 'transferability' and 'pose probe accuracy' is entirely mediated by a learned geometric model whose own biases could favor certain latent representations; the COLMAP comparison mitigates but does not eliminate this concern.

Rendering quality of transferred views degrades noticeably when target poses diverge from the context distribution (blurring/warping artifacts, FID of 5-9 vs. autoreconstruction, Table 5 evaluated only on near-distribution augmented transfers). The practical utility of the transferred renders relative to the strong TPS numbers is not fully established.

Baseline comparisons involve reimplementations of both RayZen and RUST under a modified unified setting (5 context views, L1+LPIPS loss, aggregate dataset) that differs from the originals; results in Table 4 differ substantially from published numbers. The authors justify this, but absolute comparability to prior reported results is weakened.

The stereo-monocular restriction and pairwise pose estimation limit scalability to long trajectories and wide baselines; the multi-view extension must be fine-tuned and the paper acknowledges that applying transferability training directly to multi-view models remains open.

Some important details of the augmentation scheme feel heuristic (quadrant partitioning, 5% unmasked probability) without ablation over augmentation granularity/strength, leaving unclear how sensitive the transferability objective is to this specific masking design.

strengths: The paper identifies a genuine and well-articulated conceptual gap: prior self-supervised NVS models (RayZer, RUST) learn interpolation latents rather than transferable pose representations, and the transferability criterion is a useful lens for analyzing this failure mode.

The proposed True Pose Similarity (TPS) metric is a reasonable and largely well-motivated attempt to quantify transferability, and the paper is commendably honest about its limitations (e.g., that it can be hacked and measures only geometric consistency).

The two key design insights — bootstrapping from a stereo-monocular two-view model that must extrapolate, and a pose-preserving augmentation scheme that minimizes pixel overlap while preserving camera motion — are simple, clearly explained, and plausibly effective.

Empirical evaluation is broad (four datasets spanning scenes and objects), the transferability gains over RayZer and RUST are large (e.g., >5x AUC@20°), and the ablation study (Table 3) is thorough, covering multi-view variants, bottlenecking, SE(3)/Plücker parameterization, and comparisons to SimCLR/VICReg objectives.

The appendix contains substantial reproducibility detail (architecture, optimization, compute, evaluation protocol), and robustness analyses of the pose oracles (VGGT vs. COLMAP) show awareness of evaluation pitfalls.
Limitations are candidly discussed, including wide-baseline failures, deterministic rendering artifacts, and the open problem of multi-view self-supervised training.
weaknesses: The evaluation methodology has a circularity problem that weakens the central claim: 'transferability' and 'true NVS' are defined and measured exclusively through oracle poses, and the chosen oracle is VGGT — a heavily supervised model pre-trained with strong 3D/geometry inductive biases. A paper whose narrative is that NVS should be solvable as 'pure machine learning' without geometric priors nonetheless relies on a geometry-laden pretrained model to certify that its representations are meaningful. The paper acknowledges oracle fragility but does not resolve this tension.

All baselines (RayZer, RUST) are re-implementations rather than released code, and the RUST implementation intentionally deviates from the authors' original design ('we do not leverage a set-latent scene representation'). The claimed large gaps in Table 1 therefore cannot be fully verified against published numbers, and the re-implementation choices could disadvantage the baselines; the autoencoding comparison in Table 4 also explicitly differs from RayZer's original setup.

Rendering quality is modest: PSNR around 23–26 and visible blurring/warping artifacts are acknowledged even for in-distribution targets. The paper reframes this as a deterministic-model limitation, but a 'true NVS model' with substantially degraded perceptual quality has questionable practical significance relative to supervised or oracle-based methods.

The information-leakage argument for the augmentation scheme is not airtight: masked pairs may still share substantial scene content (e.g., unmasked quadrants, global illumination and layout cues), and there is no analysis quantifying how much residual pixel information the pose latent can smuggle. The claim that XFactor 'eliminates' the cheating path is stronger than the evidence provided.

The 'first true NVS' / 'first fully self-supervised' framing is repeated aggressively and is somewhat rhetorical: whether transferability is the 'key criterion' for true NVS is a definitional position, not an established fact, and closely related ideas (CroCo-style stereo pretraining, latent action models) are discussed but the novelty boundary could be sharper.

Several claims rest on relatively thin evidence: the pose probe (Table 2) shows latents correlate with oracle poses, but the link between 'transferability' and downstream user-controllable NVS usefulness is demonstrated only qualitatively and via a self-evaluation protocol (Table 5) that the baselines cannot be run under, limiting comparability.

The scope of the method is narrow in practice: POSEENC is restricted to two-view stereo with limited baselines, multi-view capability is obtained only by pairwise chaining at fine-tuning, and transfer degrades as target poses diverge from the context distribution — significant constraints for real NVS applications.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated conceptual contribution: the paper identifies 'transferability' as the defining property of true NVS, formalizes it within a clean latent-variable decomposition of NVS systems, and shows precisely why prior self-supervised pose-free models (RayZer, RUST) fail it. This framing is genuinely insightful and elevates the work beyond a system paper.

Introduces True Pose Similarity (TPS), a reusable standardized metric for quantifying transferability, along with a careful discussion of its failure modes (e.g., hacking via replaying context sequences) and a perceptual complement.

Technically interesting method: bootstrapping from a stereo-monocular two-view model that extrapolates by design, plus a pose-preserving augmentation scheme that enables a transferability objective with real-world video. The counter-intuitive finding that explicit SE(3) parameterization of poses degrades transferability is a notable empirical insight.

Large-scale and fairly comprehensive evaluation: four real-world datasets (RE10K, DL3DV, MVImgNet, CO3Dv2) spanning scenes and objects, comparisons against two strong recent self-supervised baselines, pose probing experiments, an autoencoding benchmark for completeness, and unusually thorough ablations (bottleneck vs. unconstrained latents, SE(3)+Plücker, additional context views, SimCLR/VICReg objectives, robustness to temporal-shift corruption).

Honest treatment of evaluation validity: analysis of oracle fragility (VGGT vs. COLMAP) with quantitative justification (Tables 8-9), acknowledgment of COLMAP's high rejection rate on transferred videos, and a candid limitations section covering wide-baseline constraints and rendering artifacts.
Well written and clearly organized; the formalization in Secs. 3.1-3.3 makes the claims precise and testable.
weaknesses: Key baselines (RayZer, RUST) are author re-implementations rather than released code, and the RUST variant deviates from the original (scene encoder absorbed into a multi-view PoseEnc, full-to-partial objective). While the authors argue the comparison is still favorable to RUST and claim RayZer's authors confirmed faithfulness, some performance gaps could stem from implementation or tuning differences rather than the core design.

The central claim of 'no 3D inductive biases' is somewhat overstated: the stereo-monocular bottleneck, the disjoint-mask augmentation scheme, and the transfer objective all encode strong assumptions (e.g., that masked pairs share identical camera pose, that content overlap should be minimized). The paper is really about replacing explicit geometric parameterization with different structural priors, and the framing occasionally oversells purity.

TPS evaluation depends on a pretrained oracle (VGGT), which itself was trained with massive geometric supervision; the paper's 'pure machine learning' narrative applies only to training, and the metric's robustness, while analyzed, introduces an external dependency into the headline result.

Rendering quality under transfer is comparatively weakly evaluated: Table 5 uses pose-preserving augmentations at inference, which only XFactor can handle (baselines were not trained with masked inputs), so there is no apples-to-apples perceptual comparison of transferred rendering quality against RayZer/RUST; FID is the only shared perceptual metric and is a coarse one.

The method is deterministic and exhibits blur/warping artifacts on out-of-distribution target poses; absolute rendering fidelity lags oracle-supervised systems, and the proposed remedy (integrating generative models) is left to future work.

Some novelty overlap with prior ideas: stereo/monocular bootstrapping echoes CroCo-style pre-training, and the transferability objective is related to cross-sequence consistency ideas in latent action models; the contribution is a careful synthesis and analysis rather than a fundamentally new mechanism, which slightly tempers the 'first' claim.

Several details that affect reproducibility (exact augmentation statistics, heuristic baseline selection of 100/12/12/20 frames, dataset mixing ratios) are deferred to the appendix and only briefly described; no code release is mentioned.
